slides.heading: Oral Lesson
bullets: “A man of wealth rode by our house.” — the group *of wealth* modifies the noun *man*:  an adjective element.
The group *by our house* modifies the verb *rode*; it tells where he rode:  an adverbial element.
*of* connects the noun *wealth* to the noun *man*; *by* connects the noun *house* with the verb *rode*.
They show the relations between the words which they connect, and are called *Prepositions*.
The nouns which follow them, *wealth* and *house*, are called their *Objects*.

slides.text: A Preposition is a word used to show the relation between its object and some other word.
examples: But “He rode **by**.” — no object:  *by* is an adverb.

slides.heading: The Principal Prepositions
bullets: a · aboard · about · above · according to · across · after · against · along · amid(st) · among(st) · around · as to · at · athwart
before · behind · beneath · beside(s) · between · betwixt · beyond · but · by · down · during · ere · except · for · from
in · into · of · off · on · over · past · round · save · since · till · until · through · throughout
to · toward(s) · under · unto · up · upon · with · within · without
Glosses:  *a* = at, on, in (twice *a* day);  *athwart* = across;  *betwixt* = between;  *ere* = before;  *save*, *but* = except (all *but* one);  *unto* = to.

slides.heading: Practice — Find the Prepositions (Set 1)
slides.instruction: Name each preposition, its object, and the word it relates its object to.  Model — “He came from France to America.” — from:  France → came;  to:  America → came.
items: The boy went through the gate into the garden.
Be not forward in the presence of your superiors.
He drove over the bridge into the city.
He went to the doctor for advice.
answers: through:  gate → went;  into:  garden → went
in:  presence → forward;  of:  superiors → presence
over:  bridge → drove;  into:  city → drove
to:  doctor → went;  for:  advice → went

slides.heading: Practice — Find the Prepositions (Set 2)
slides.instruction: Name each preposition, its object, and the word it relates its object to.  Model — “He came from France to America.” — from:  France → came;  to:  America → came.
items: The path brought them to the end of the wood.
She turned to the old man with a lovely smile upon her face.
The light came through the stained windows of the old church.
answers: to:  end → brought;  of:  wood → end
to:  man → turned;  with:  smile → turned;  upon:  face → smile
through:  windows → came;  of:  church → windows

slides.text: A group of words consisting of a preposition and its object is called a Phrase.
examples: The ship was driven **upon the rocks**.
The sleep **of a laboring man** is sweet.

slides.heading: Phrases as Elements
bullets: Phrases are most commonly used as adjective or adverbial elements.
“Habits of industry” — *of industry* modifies the noun *Habits*:  an adjective element.
“will lead to prosperity” — *to prosperity* modifies the verb *will lead*:  an adverbial element.
A phrase is not a proposition:  it has no subject and no predicate.  *after dinner* is a phrase; *after we had dined* is a clause.

rows.sentence: Habits of industry will lead to prosperity.
rows.note: Declarative. *Habits* is the subject; *will lead*, the predicate. *Habits* is modified by the phrase *of industry*, an adjective element; *will lead*, by the phrase *to prosperity*, an adverbial element.

rows.sentence: The sleep of a laboring man is sweet.
rows.note: Declarative. *sleep* is the subject; *sweet*, the predicate; *is*, the copula. *sleep* is modified by *the* and by the phrase *of a laboring man*, both adjective elements. *man* is modified by *a* and *laboring*, both adjective elements.

slides.heading: Practice — Adjective or Adverbial?
slides.instruction: Name each phrase, the word it modifies, and the element it is.
items: The young lambs are bleating in the meadows.
The roof of the old barn leaked.
The two thieves divided the money between them.
They came to the country of the free.
Our sincerest laughter is fraught with some pain.
The leaves of the oak fell in the night.
answers: in the meadows → are bleating:  adverbial
of the old barn → roof:  adjective
between them → divided:  adverbial
to the country → came:  adverbial;  of the free → country:  adjective
with some pain → fraught:  adverbial
of the oak → leaves:  adjective;  in the night → fell:  adverbial

slides.heading: Practice — Replace the Phrase
slides.instruction: Put a single word or a clause in place of each phrase.  Model — “Henry studies his lessons with care” = “Henry studies his lessons carefully.”  “Ice forms in cold weather” = “Ice forms when the weather is cold.”
items: The sailors weighed anchor at sunrise.
The enraged lion struggled in vain.
Flowers bloom in the spring.
I have written this letter in haste.
Our schools should be the pride and boast of our country.
The face of the poor boy was disfigured.
answers: when the sun rose  (or:  early)
vainly
when spring comes
hastily
our country’s pride and boast
The poor boy’s face

slides.heading: Oral Lesson — The Infinitive
bullets: “To play is pleasant.” — *to play* is the subject.  Why?  It is that of which something is affirmed.
It is a form of the verb *play*.  It expresses action, but does not affirm it.
For this reason it is called an *Infinitive*, or an *infinitive Phrase*.

slides.text: An Infinitive is a form of the verb used to express action without affirming it.
examples: The lawyer went to his office **to write** a letter.

rows.label: Subject
rows.text: that of which something is affirmed

rows.label: Predicate
rows.text: that which is affirmed of the subject

rows.label: Objective
rows.text: an objective element: completes the meaning of a verb

rows.label: Adverbial
rows.text: an adverbial element: modifies a verb, adjective, or adverb
rows.examples: I came **to see** you.  ·  He is glad **to help**.

rows.label: Adjective
rows.text: an adjective element: modifies a noun

slides.heading: The Sign of the Infinitive
bullets: The word *to* is usually placed before the verb, and is called the *sign of the infinitive*.
The two parts should not be separated in analyzing or parsing:  *to play* is one element.
This *to* is not a preposition:  it has no object.  In “to go to the city,” only the second *to* is a preposition.
An infinitive affirms nothing.  In “To love is to obey,” the copula *is* does the affirming.

rows.note: Declarative. *To love* is the subject; *to obey*, the predicate; *is*, the copula.

rows.sentence: The lawyer went to his office to write a letter.
rows.note: Declarative. *lawyer* is the subject; *went*, the predicate. *lawyer* is modified by *the*, an adjective element; *went*, by the phrases *to his office* and *to write a letter*, both adverbial elements. *office* is modified by *his*, an adjective element; *to write*, by *letter*, an objective element, which is modified by *a*, an adjective element.

slides.heading: Practice — The Infinitive’s Office
slides.instruction: Name each infinitive, and tell whether it is a subject, a predicate, or an adjective, objective, or adverbial element.
items: To lie is wicked.
He wants to go to the city.
John studies to learn.
My sister wishes to remain here.
Are you ready to recite?
To teach the young is a pleasant task.
To see is to believe.
He had no reason to complain.
answers: To lie:  subject
to go:  objective
to learn:  adverbial (→ studies)
to remain:  objective
to recite:  adverbial (→ ready)
To teach:  subject
To see:  subject;  to believe:  predicate
to complain:  adjective (→ reason)

slides.heading: The Position of Modifiers
bullets: The meaning of a sentence may often be changed by changing the position of its words, phrases, and clauses.
“John **only** studies algebra.” — *only* modifies *John*:  he is the only person that studies algebra.
“John studies algebra **only**.” — *only* modifies *algebra*:  it is the only branch John studies.
Rule. — Words, phrases, and clauses, used as modifiers, should be placed as near the modified words as possible.

slides.heading: Misplaced Phrases & Clauses
bullets: “A watch was found yesterday by a school-boy **with steel hands**.” — the steel hands belong to the school-boy!
Say:  “A watch **with steel hands** was found yesterday by a school-boy.”
“He needs no spectacles **that can not see**.” — the clause is meant to modify *He*, not *spectacles*.
Say:  “He **that can not see** needs no spectacles.”

slides.heading: Practice — Place the Phrases
slides.instruction: Locate the phrases properly in these sentences.
items: The sled was bought by a boy going to school for a dollar.
The book was dropped by a bad boy on my head.
I saw a dog bite a man with long ears and a white spot on his face.
answers: The sled was bought for a dollar by a boy going to school.
The book was dropped on my head by a bad boy.
I saw a dog with long ears and a white spot on its face bite a man.

slides.heading: Practice — Place the Clauses
slides.instruction: Locate the clauses properly in these sentences.
items: Mr. Otis needs a surgeon, who has broken his arm.
A silver fruit knife was found by a child which has a broken back.
He wants no food that can not eat.
answers: Mr. Otis, who has broken his arm, needs a surgeon.
A silver fruit knife which has a broken back was found by a child.
He that can not eat wants no food.
